questions.stem: Which form suits this task's requirement that the imaginative text be predominantly prose?
options: a verse novel told in free verse
a dramatic monologue in blank verse
a ballad that tells a long narrative
a short story or a chapter of a novel
questions.explanation: The syllabus asks for an imaginative form that is predominantly prose, such as a short story, memoir, interior monologue, novel chapter, drama script or screenplay. Verse novels, blank-verse monologues and ballads tell stories, but they are verse forms.

questions.stem: Which story best suits the purpose 'to satirise'?
options: one gently poking fun at a family's chaotic morning routine for warm laughs
one realistically depicting an influencer's private anxiety with sympathy
one imitating a famous author's style closely as an affectionate tribute
one exaggerating a wellness influencer's habits to expose an empty industry
questions.explanation: Satire uses exaggeration and irony to expose folly or vice, as in ridiculing an industry through its excesses. Gentle family comedy amuses without exposing anything, sympathetic realism invites understanding, and affectionate imitation is pastiche or homage.

questions.stem: Which choice best suits the purpose 'to disconcert' readers?
options: a fast-paced chase in which the hero narrowly escapes from danger
a mystery in which the detective calmly explains every clue at the end
a melancholy reflection on a lost childhood home, softly nostalgic in tone
a calm domestic narration in which small details reveal something is wrong
questions.explanation: To disconcert is to unsettle, and ordinary surfaces that gradually reveal wrongness create unease. A chase thrills, a mystery that explains every clue reassures, and nostalgia saddens rather than unsettles.

questions.stem: Which story best suits the purpose 'to explore'?
options: one persuading readers that young people should leave home at eighteen
one recounting a character's move away in a detailed, factual sequence
one following a character's uncertain thoughts about leaving home, unresolved
one showing a character leaving home and learning a clear lesson about family
questions.explanation: An exploratory text investigates an idea or experience without needing to settle it. A neatly learnt lesson, a persuasive case or a factual recount serves other purposes.

questions.stem: A story about a grandmother's death is told with gentle humour. The purpose is most likely to:
options: make the story a comedy in which the death is incidental
celebrate her life while acknowledging the loss
satirise the family's grief as excessive and false
distract readers from the loss until the final scene
questions.explanation: Gentle humour in a story of loss often honours a life and its character while still registering grief. It is affectionate rather than satirical, and it keeps the loss in view rather than hiding or sidelining it.

questions.stem: When deciding on subject matter for this task, a writer should mainly consider:
options: what best suits her purpose, intended effect and chosen genre
what she knows most about, so the story will be accurate and detailed
whatever is most dramatic, since a strong subject carries the writing
what her intended audience already knows well, so nothing needs explaining
questions.explanation: The task asks students to choose subject matter and genre that best suit their purpose. Familiarity, drama or what readers already know may help, but they do not decide whether a subject serves the writing.

questions.stem: A writer wants to critique a society's obsession with surveillance. Which genre most suits this purpose?
options: historical fiction
gothic fiction
dystopian fiction
utopian fiction
questions.explanation: Dystopian fiction imagines a society in which present tendencies are pushed to an extreme, which suits critique of surveillance. Utopian fiction imagines an ideal society, and historical and gothic fiction do not lend themselves to that kind of social warning.

questions.stem: A writer depicts teenagers in her story as thoughtful and politically engaged rather than apathetic. This mainly:
options: represents teenagers objectively, as they really are today
challenges a common representation and repositions readers
reflects the dominant representation of teenagers in the media
satirises political teenagers by exaggerating their earnestness
questions.explanation: The task asks how an imaginative text shapes representations to position audiences, and showing teenagers against a stereotype challenges that stereotype. Nothing signals satire, and no representation is simply objective.

questions.stem: A writer wants her story to question the assumption that success means wealth. Which choice would best position readers?
options: a wealthy, admired character whose emptiness shows in small private moments
a narrator who tells readers directly that money cannot buy happiness
a wealthy villain whose greed is punished by ruin at the end of the story
a rags-to-riches plot in which hard work earns a fortune and respect
questions.explanation: Revealing emptiness behind admired wealth lets readers draw the conclusion themselves, which positions them more powerfully than a stated moral. Punishing a villain's greed condemns greed rather than questioning success, and a rags-to-riches plot reinforces the assumption.

questions.stem: With a 2000-word limit, the most effective approach is usually to:
options: use many short scenes so that the pace never slows down
develop a few key moments and characters in depth
cover several years, summarising the time between scenes
open with a full page of backstory to establish the world
questions.explanation: A short form rewards focus, so a few moments rendered fully have more impact than a sprawling plot. Summarising years, front-loading backstory or racing through many scenes dilutes the effect.

questions.stem: Focalisation refers to:
options: whose perception filters what the narrative shows
who tells the story and in which grammatical person
the point in a plot where the main conflict comes into focus
the narrator's distance in time from the events being told
questions.explanation: Focalisation is about whose eyes and mind the narrative sees through, which may differ from who narrates. Who tells the story, and in which person, is narration, and the other options describe plot and temporal distance.

questions.stem: A story is narrated in the third person, but every event is filtered through what a seven-year-old notices. In narrative terms, the child is the:
options: focaliser
narrator
implied author
first-person narrator
questions.explanation: The narrator is the third-person voice telling the story, but the child's perception shapes what is shown, so the child is the focaliser. A first-person narrator would tell the story as 'I', and the implied author is the sense of authorship behind the whole text.

questions.stem: A writer drafts a story about a flood with omniscient narration, then revises it to focalise only through the family dog. The revision most likely:
options: adds comic relief that lightens the disaster for its readers
makes the disaster strange and poignant through limited perception
makes the dog an unreliable narrator whose account readers must reject
turns the story into an allegory in which the dog stands for humanity
questions.explanation: A dog's limited understanding defamiliarises the flood, so readers piece together what it cannot grasp, which can be deeply moving. The dog focalises rather than narrates, nothing makes it stand for humanity, and the effect is poignant rather than comic.

questions.stem: A story is narrated by a pompous, self-satisfied character whose words reveal more than he intends. This creates:
options: suspense, as readers wait for him to discover the truth
irony, as readers judge him beyond his own understanding
sarcasm, as the narrator mocks the other characters' failings
empathy, as readers come to share his flattering view of himself
questions.explanation: When a narrator unwittingly exposes himself, readers see more than he does, which is a form of irony. Sarcasm is deliberate mockery, readers do not share his view, and the effect depends on judgement rather than suspense.

questions.stem: A writer wants readers both to empathise with her protagonist and to judge her critically. Which combination best achieves this?
options: first-person narration, so that readers trust her version of events
chapters narrated by other characters, who criticise her directly
a tragic backstory revealed early, so that readers forgive her faults
close focalisation for empathy, with ironic details exposing her blind spots
questions.explanation: Close access to a character builds sympathy, while details she misreads let readers stand back and judge. Trusting her version removes judgement, others' criticism without her perspective removes empathy, and a backstory that excuses her invites forgiveness rather than critique.

questions.stem: To signal that a narrator is unreliable without stating it, a writer could:
options: reveal the narrator's lies in an epilogue told by another character
let other characters' reactions contradict the narrator's account
write the narration in the third person to create some distance
make the narrator a likeable character who is candid with readers
questions.explanation: Subtle signals, such as others reacting in ways that do not fit the narrator's version, let readers infer unreliability. Third-person narration does not signal it, likeable candour works against it, and an epilogue that exposes the lies states it outright.

questions.stem: A story about failing a final-year exam is told in the second person to the narrator's younger self ('You open the envelope'). This choice most likely:
options: signals an unreliable narrator who refuses to admit the failure as hers
creates both intimacy and distance as the narrator faces a former self
casts the reader as the student, so the exam becomes the reader's own
makes the narration omniscient, as the older self knows each outcome
questions.explanation: Addressing a past self as 'you' is close and personal yet sets that self at a remove, dramatising reflection on who one was. The 'you' is the younger self rather than the reader, hindsight is not omniscience, and the form faces the failure rather than disowning it.

questions.stem: A story about a marriage begins with the divorce papers and moves backwards to the couple's first meeting. The reverse chronology most likely:
options: makes the hopeful ending poignant, since readers know what comes later
builds suspense about whether the couple will end up divorcing
creates a circular structure that returns readers to the divorce
uses foreshadowing to hint at the divorce before it happens
questions.explanation: Knowing the outcome first colours the hopeful early meeting with sadness. Suspense about the divorce is removed, the story ends at the meeting rather than circling back, and the divorce is shown first rather than hinted at.

questions.stem: A writer cuts her story's opening three pages of backstory and begins at the moment a stranger knocks on the door. The main benefit is that:
options: readers are drawn in at once, with backstory woven in later
the story gains mystery because the past is left out for good
the story becomes a flashback narrative told in reverse order
the opening now uses a frame narrative to introduce the main story
questions.explanation: Starting at a moment of tension engages readers immediately, and essential history can be revealed as needed. Backstory is relocated, not lost, and beginning in the action involves neither reverse order nor a frame.

questions.stem: A frame narrative is:
options: a story that opens in the middle of the action
a story within a story, introduced by an outer narrative
a story that begins and ends with the same scene or image
a story told through a series of letters, diaries or documents
questions.explanation: A frame narrative uses an outer story to introduce and contain an inner one, as when a character begins telling a tale. A matching beginning and end is a circular structure, documents make an epistolary form, and opening mid-action is in medias res.

questions.stem: A story ends with the same sentence it began with, but by the end readers understand that sentence differently. This technique mainly:
options: uses the line as a motif that symbolises the story's central theme
transforms the repeated line's meaning through what the story has revealed
creates a frame narrative, with the story nested inside the sentence
shows that the characters end exactly where they began, unchanged
questions.explanation: Repetition at both ends invites comparison, and what readers have learned changes how the line lands. A repeated sentence is not a frame or a motif in itself, and the device shapes meaning rather than signalling stasis.

questions.stem: To slow the pace at a crucial moment, a writer would most likely:
options: expand a few seconds into detailed sensory description and thought
use short, fragmented sentences to heighten the moment's tension
switch to rapid dialogue so that readers hear each word spoken
jump ahead in time to show the consequences of the moment
questions.explanation: Lingering on detail and thought makes narrative time slow down relative to story time. Short fragments and rapid dialogue speed the pace, and a time jump skips the moment altogether.

questions.stem: In a story, a broken clock appears once, at the moment a character learns of a death. This is best described as:
options: a symbol, a single object charged with meaning
a motif, an object charged with thematic meaning
foreshadowing, a hint of the death to come
pathetic fallacy, an object mirroring her grief
questions.explanation: A single object that carries meaning at a key moment is a symbol. A motif recurs, which this clock does not; foreshadowing hints at what is still to come; and pathetic fallacy gives human feeling to nature or weather.

questions.stem: A writer repeats an image of migrating birds three times: at a departure, midway through, and at a homecoming. For the motif to work well, the image should:
options: keep one fixed meaning so that readers recognise it each time
be explained by the narrator at first, then left to speak for itself
appear at random, unconnected moments so that it feels natural
gather meaning as the story develops, linking key moments
questions.explanation: A motif works when its recurrences connect moments and accumulate significance. A fixed meaning cannot grow, explaining it flattens it, and random placement fails to link key moments.

questions.stem: To create a mood of creeping unease in a suburban setting, the most effective choice is:
options: dark, stormy weather and a howling wind around the houses
a narrator who tells readers plainly that she felt a growing sense of unease all day
ordinary details that are slightly wrong, like a sprinkler running in the rain
a sudden, violent event in the very first line, designed to shock readers
questions.explanation: Mood is built through detail, and small wrongnesses in a familiar setting unsettle readers without announcement. A sudden shock is not creeping, stock storm imagery is a cliche, and stating a feeling does not create a mood.

questions.stem: A story set entirely in a hospital car park overnight most likely uses setting to:
options: create a neutral backdrop that keeps the focus on dialogue
reflect the characters' moods through pathetic fallacy
confine the characters, intensifying their conflict
symbolise the characters' journey towards healing
questions.explanation: A single, constrained setting traps characters together and compresses time, which raises tension. It is active rather than neutral, and nothing suggests a symbol of healing or weather mirroring mood.

questions.stem: Which line characterises most economically?
options: She tipped the waiter in exact change, and counted it twice.
She was careful with money, the kind who checks each bill twice.
Her thin lips, cold grey eyes and neat bun spoke of a mean nature.
She was mean, careful, suspicious, thrifty and rather unfriendly.
questions.explanation: One telling action reveals both carefulness and meanness without stating either. The other lines name her traits, directly or through stock physical description.

questions.stem: In a short story, which dialogue choice best reveals a strained relationship?
options: long speeches in which each character explains exactly how they feel
dialect and slang that show the characters come from different places
polite, formal speech, with a narrator explaining the tension beneath
terse exchanges about trivial things while the real issue goes unspoken
questions.explanation: What characters avoid saying can reveal tension powerfully, so clipped talk around the real issue creates subtext. Explaining feelings, in speech or narration, spells the tension out instead of dramatising it, and dialect shows origin rather than strain.

questions.stem: A story tells of a friendship's end entirely in the form of an obituary. This choice:
options: creates a frame narrative around the story of the friendship
is a parody that mocks the conventions of the obituary form
signals that one of the two friends has literally died
exploits a familiar form to create irony and fresh meaning
questions.explanation: Borrowing the obituary's conventions for a living friendship creates irony and frames the ending as a kind of death. It uses the form rather than mocking it, there is no outer story, and nobody has literally died.

questions.stem: A story titled 'Instructions for Leaving' most likely:
options: announces the story's moral, which the ending will confirm
identifies the protagonist's main goal, which the plot will achieve
sets up expectations of form and theme the story can play against
signals that the story will be a satire of self-help books
questions.explanation: A title can frame how readers approach a story, here suggesting both an instructional form and a theme of departure. It sets up expectations to play against rather than announcing a target, a moral or a goal.

questions.stem: A student's story aims 'to subvert' heroic war narratives. Which combination best serves that purpose?
options: a historical account of a real battle, told from the point of view of a general
a heroic quest's conventions, with a victory shown to be hollow and costly
a parody that mocks the soldiers themselves as cowardly, foolish and vain
a tragic hero whose noble death inspires his comrades to victory
questions.explanation: Subversion uses a genre's familiar conventions and then undermines them, so a hollow victory inside a heroic structure turns the form against itself. Mocking soldiers targets people rather than the narrative, a noble, inspiring death reinforces the convention, and a historical account is not imaginative subversion.

questions.stem: A long, breathless sentence piling clause on clause during a chase scene mainly:
options: is a periodic sentence that withholds its main clause
builds a tricolon that gives the chase a formal balance
mimics the urgency and momentum of the action
slows the action down so readers notice each detail
questions.explanation: Syntax can enact what it describes, and an accumulating sentence carries readers forward with the chase. It speeds rather than slows the action, and piling up clauses is neither periodic nor balanced.

questions.stem: The 'implied author' is:
options: the narrating voice that tells the story, in any person
the reader that the text seems to address and expect
the author and values that readers infer from the whole text
the real author's intentions, as stated in interviews or notes
questions.explanation: The implied author is the sense of an author, and of the values behind the text, that readers construct from the work itself. It is distinct from the real person's stated intentions, from any narrator and from the implied reader.

questions.stem: Which revision decision best shows editorial independence?
options: accepting each change a peer suggests, to show openness to feedback
keeping the first draft unchanged to preserve its original spontaneity
adding techniques until the story shows each one studied in class
cutting a favourite descriptive passage because it slows the climax
questions.explanation: Editorial independence means judging one's own draft critically, even when that means cutting something one likes. Accepting every suggestion, refusing to revise or cramming in techniques shows no independent critical judgement.

questions.stem: Writing the task as a screenplay for a short film requires conveying characters' inner lives mainly through:
options: voice-over narration describing what each character is thinking
detailed scene directions describing each character's feelings
camera directions such as close-ups specified for each line
action, dialogue and visual detail rather than narrated thoughts
questions.explanation: Screenplays present what can be seen and heard, so inner life is shown through behaviour, speech and images. Constant voice-over and directions describing feelings tell rather than show, and screenwriters leave most camera choices to the director.
